notes.meaning: Here begins a new section of Jeremiah: God's messages about the other nations. It runs through chapter 51. The nations around Israel did not know God, but He is still their King and Judge. He will hold them to account too.

The first message is about Egypt. Pharaoh Neco had killed good King Josiah of Judah at Megiddo. About four years later, Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon crushed Neco's army at Carchemish, by the Euphrates River, around 605 BC. Egypt lost all its land between the Nile and the Euphrates, and Josiah's death did not go unpunished.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think verses 3-12 are a song written after the battle, not a prediction made before it. Keil and Delitzsch argue that it is a true prophecy.

notes.meaning: The prophet mockingly calls Egypt's army to get ready. They are to grab the small and large shields, hitch the horses to the chariots, and put on helmets. They are to sharpen their spears and put on armor. Every piece of gear is listed, so by human standards they look sure to win. Yet all this preparation will count for nothing against God.

Suddenly, in a vision, Jeremiah sees this mighty army panic and run. They flee so fast they dare not even look back. "Terror on every side" is one of Jeremiah's favorite phrases. It also gives the answer to his question: God Himself is bringing this judgment.

Neither speed nor strength will save them. Even the fastest runners and the bravest soldiers will stumble and fall far to the north, by the Euphrates. The race is not always won by the swift, nor the battle by the strong.

Each year the Nile floods its banks and covers Egypt's land. In the same way, Egypt's army swells with pride and boasts it will cover the earth and destroy cities. The prophet makes fun of this boasting. Like the Nile, the army will go back as fast as it came.

Again the prophet mockingly cheers them on: charge, horses and chariots! Egypt had hired soldiers from Cush (Ethiopia), Put (Libya) and Lud, who were skilled with shields and bows. Such a large army with foreign help seemed impossible to beat. Still, it would fall.

Egypt thought this would be its big day, but the day belongs to God. It is a day of payback, partly for the killing of Josiah. The sword "drinking blood" is a picture of a huge slaughter. Calling it a "sacrifice" shows that God's judgment here is right and just.

Gilead was famous for a healing ointment called balm. Jeremiah tells Egypt, with irony, to go get some, because no medicine will heal this wound. "Virgin" means Egypt had never yet been conquered. Egypt would not disappear as a nation, but it would never regain its old strength.
News of Egypt's shameful defeat spreads to every nation, and its cries fill the earth. In the panic, soldiers crash into each other and fall together. Their huge numbers become a trap for them.

A second message begins. It is about something that happened years later: Nebuchadnezzar attacking Egypt itself. Egypt had been beaten abroad, but it still felt safe at home. Now the war would come to its own land.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some historians once doubted that Nebuchadnezzar ever invaded Egypt. Later, an inscription and Babylonian records were found that describe a campaign in his 37th year (about 568-567 BC).

notes.meaning: The warning is to be shouted in Egypt's border towns and in the great city of Memphis. Egypt's neighbors have already fallen, so Egypt should get ready, though getting ready will not help. These were the very towns where Jewish refugees had settled against God's command. They would learn what a poor hiding place Egypt was.
Why were Egypt's strong warriors swept away? They could not stand because the Lord pushed them down. Egypt was not fighting only Babylon. It was fighting God.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The old Greek translation reads, "Why did Apis flee?" Apis was Egypt's sacred bull-god. Many scholars follow this reading, so the verse shows Israel's God beating Egypt's god. Keil and Delitzsch do not accept it.

notes.meaning: Soldiers keep stumbling over one another. The foreign fighters Egypt had hired say, "Let's go home to our own people, away from this sword." Soldiers who fight only for pay are not much use when real trouble comes.

People call Pharaoh "all noise": big talk and no action. Some think he missed the time he had set to come and fight. Others think he wasted the time of grace God had given him to turn back. Great talkers are often little doers.

God, the true King, makes a solemn promise by His own life. Mount Tabor towers over the hills around it, and Mount Carmel stands high above the sea. In the same way, Nebuchadnezzar will tower over Egypt. What God has decided is as fixed as those mountains.

Egypt had lived in comfort and safety. Now it is told to pack for exile, which means being taken away from home as captives. Even the great city of Memphis will be left in ruins with no one living there. We should prepare our hearts for hard times too.

Egypt is like a beautiful, well-fed young cow, proud and never trained to the yoke. But a stinging fly is coming from the north, meaning Babylon. Some think the cow picture pokes fun at the bull and cow gods Egypt worshiped.

Even Egypt's hired soldiers are like fattened calves. They are well fed and soft from easy living, and they look fattened for slaughter. They will turn and run, because their day of trouble and punishment has come.

Once Egypt bellowed like a proud cow. Now it will only make a low hiss, like a snake slipping away, too afraid to cry out. The Babylonians will come with axes, like woodcutters chopping trees that cannot fight back.
Egypt's "forest" stands for its many people, cities and leaders. However thick it seems, it will be cut down. The enemy army will be more than a swarm of locusts, too many to count.
Now the picture is said plainly. Egypt will be put to shame and handed over to the people of the north, the Babylonians.

God names who He will punish. Amon was the chief god of Thebes, Egypt's famous city. God will also punish Pharaoh, Egypt's other gods and rulers, and everyone who trusts in Pharaoh. That includes the Jews who ran to Egypt and trusted Pharaoh instead of God.

Egypt will be handed over to Nebuchadnezzar and his officers. But God also says that later Egypt will be lived in again as before. Ezekiel spoke of this coming after forty years. God judges Egypt but does not wipe it out, and in this His mercy shows even toward other nations.

While the nations shake, God comforts His people: "Don't be afraid." He calls Israel "my servant" because He chose them, not because they earned it. He promises to bring them home from far away to rest and safety, and to be with them. He will wipe out nations, but never His own people. He will still correct them "justly," meaning in fair measure, for their good and only for a time.

differ.view: The Jewish nation as a nation has ended, but this promise finds its full meaning in the gospel church. The church is God's spiritual Israel, and He will never bring it to an end.
The Jews have survived as a distinct people while their old enemies vanished. This is a sign that Israel will one day be restored to God's favor, when the time of the Gentiles is fulfilled.
The promise of a peaceful return looks ahead to a future kingdom age for Israel that has not come yet.
